title: Resource Hierarchy and Governance (Advanced): Governance at Scale
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Design a management group hierarchy based on the Azure landing zone architecture, and explain why it follows workload types instead of the org chart.
- Explain why subscriptions are the unit of scale, what subscription vending automates, and at which scope RBAC, budgets and policies belong.
- Run policy-driven governance at management-group scope: where definitions live, safe rollout, remediation identities and exemptions (Waiver vs Mitigated).
- Manage governance as code and plan the move from Azure Blueprints to deployment stacks and template specs.
- Use Azure Resource Graph and Azure Arc to see and govern every subscription — and the servers that will never move to Azure.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

A year after the storefront moved to Azure, Nusantara Retail has seven subscriptions: storefront production and test, the loyalty app, finance's data warehouse, a shared network hub, and two that nobody quite remembers creating — one of them is the Visual Studio subscription Dewi uses for experiments. Next month the company completes the purchase of a twelve-store chain in Sulawesi, which brings two more subscriptions with resources in West Europe. And each of the forty stores still runs a small point-of-sale server in its back office that will never move to the cloud.

The guardrails you built in Lunch 18 protect exactly one subscription. Everything else was configured by hand, a little differently each time. Rizky's old blueprint, which stamped tags and roles onto new subscriptions, stops accepting new assignments at the end of this month.

Ibu Sari puts it plainly: "Next year we will have twenty subscriptions. How do we make every one of them follow the same rules from the minute it exists — without you configuring each one by hand?"

Reading

1. A hierarchy designed for policy, not for the org chart

In Lunch 04 you met the resource hierarchy: a Microsoft Entra tenant, the tenant root group at the top, management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources. Anything you assign at a scope — a role or a policy — flows down to everything beneath it, and costs roll up. At small scale you barely notice the top of that tree. At company scale it becomes your most important design decision, because inheritance is how one rule reaches twenty subscriptions.

A few platform facts shape the design. A management group tree can be six levels deep, not counting the tenant root or the subscription level. Below the root, every management group and subscription has exactly one parent. The tenant root group's ID is the tenant ID, and you can neither move nor delete it. A management group's ID is permanent once created; only its display name can change. By default, any user in the tenant can create management groups, and every new subscription lands directly under the tenant root group — outside all of your carefully designed rules.

The Azure landing zone architecture from the Cloud Adoption Framework gives you a proven starting shape. At the time of writing (October 2026) it recommends these management groups:

Management group | What lives there | Typical guardrails
Intermediate root (your prefix, for example nusa) | Everything the company governs; sits just below the tenant root group | The company-wide baseline: allowed regions, required tags, security benchmark
Platform → Security, Management, Connectivity, Identity | One dedicated subscription each for SIEM tooling, central logging, the hub network and identity services | Rules for shared infrastructure, managed by the platform team
Landing zones → Corp, Online, Local | Workload subscriptions: Corp for apps that need the corporate network, Online for internet-facing apps, Local for workloads on Azure Local clusters | Workload-agnostic security rules at the parent, archetype-specific rules below
Sandboxes | Subscriptions for learning and experiments, isolated from the corporate network | A lighter policy set and strict budgets
Decommissioned | Cancelled landing zones waiting to be deleted | Deny almost everything new

Notice what is missing. There is no "Finance" or "Marketing" management group, because a department change should not force you to rewire policies. There are no "Production" and "Development" groups either: environments are separate subscriptions inside the same management group, so test is governed exactly like production. Regions do not get their own groups unless a data residency or sovereignty rule genuinely differs between them. The guidance is to keep the tree flat — three or four levels — and to group subscriptions by the rules they need, which the landing zone architecture calls workload archetypes.

Two settings complete the picture. In the hierarchy settings, choose a default management group for new subscriptions (Sandboxes is a good candidate), so a Visual Studio subscription like Dewi's starts under the sandbox rules instead of escaping them. And turn on the setting that requires authorization to create management groups, so only the platform team can reshape the tree.

Tip: Never hang your baseline directly on the tenant root group. An intermediate root gives you a scope you can rename, test against (a second, small "canary" hierarchy is common) and even replace, while the tenant root stays almost empty. It also keeps an acquired company's subscriptions out of your rules until you deliberately move them in.

2. Subscriptions as units of scale — and vending them

If management groups are the folders, subscriptions are the units you hand out. Each one is a boundary for billing, for service quotas and limits, for access, and for blast radius: a mistake or a runaway script in the loyalty subscription cannot exhaust the storefront's quota or wander into its resource groups. That is why mature organisations create many smaller subscriptions — usually one per workload and environment — instead of one giant one.

Creating subscriptions by hand does not scale, and every manual step is a chance to forget something. Subscription vending turns a request into a fully governed subscription through automation. A workload team fills in a form or opens a pull request; a pipeline built with Bicep or Terraform (both have ready-made vending modules) does the rest.

Creating subscriptions programmatically requires billing permissions on an Enterprise Agreement, a Microsoft Customer Agreement or a Microsoft Partner Agreement account, so the lab skips this step — extra subscriptions on a personal account are also easy to forget. The important idea is the order: the subscription is placed in the right management group before anyone deploys a workload, so inherited policies are already waiting.

The same "decide the scope once" thinking applies to everything else you assign:

Control | Best scope | Why
Company-wide policy baseline | Intermediate root | Reaches every subscription, including future ones
Archetype rules (for example "no public IPs" for Corp) | Corp or Online management group | Only the workloads that need the rule get it
Platform team access | Platform or intermediate root, activated through Privileged Identity Management | Broad rights, but only when needed and with an audit trail
Workload team access | Their subscription or resource group, granted to Entra groups | Least privilege; no inherited surprises
Budgets | Subscription for the owning team; management group for an overall view | Alerts reach the people who can act

For RBAC at scale, assign roles to Entra groups, never to individuals, and prefer built-in roles. When you need a custom role, note that its assignable scopes can include at most one management group, and roles with data actions cannot be assigned at management-group scope. Make privileged roles eligible rather than permanent with Privileged Identity Management (PIM), which needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance licences — Lunch 22 covers it in depth. For budgets at higher scopes, remember from Lunch 19 that budgets alert but never stop resources, and that management-group cost views are not available for every billing agreement type (check the Cost Management scope documentation for yours).

3. Policy-driven governance at management-group scope

In Lunch 18 you assigned three single policies to one resource group. At scale you bundle them into an initiative and assign it once, high in the tree, with parameters that let the same initiative serve different archetypes — Corp might allow only indonesiacentral, while Sandboxes also allow southeastasia. Remember from Lunch 18 that assignments stack: a resource must satisfy every assignment above it, so a lower scope can tighten a rule but never loosen one. Keep the top-level baseline short, and put stricter rules lower down.

Three rules decide whether this works in practice.

Where a definition is saved decides where it can be assigned. A custom definition saved in a subscription can only be assigned inside that subscription. One saved in a management group can be assigned to that group and anything below it. So save shared custom definitions and initiatives at the intermediate root, even if you first assign them lower down. At the time of writing, a single scope holds up to 500 custom policy definitions and 200 initiatives, and an initiative can reference up to 1,000 policies.

Roll out like software. A new assignment with a Deny effect at the intermediate root can block deployments across the whole company within minutes. Start every assignment with enforcement mode DoNotEnforce: compliance is still evaluated and reported, but nothing is denied or changed. Review the results, fix or exempt what you find, then enforce in rings — a test subscription first, then one archetype, then everything. Resource selectors and overrides on an assignment let you stage enforcement, for example region by region, without creating copies.

Remediation needs an identity with the right roles in the right places. Modify and DeployIfNotExists (DINE) assignments act on your behalf through a managed identity, either system-assigned (one per assignment) or user-assigned (created once, granted roles once, reused by many assignments). The roles come from the roleDefinitionIds in the definition. The portal grants them for you; the CLI and infrastructure-as-code deployments must grant them explicitly. Once an assignment is enforced, new and updated resources are fixed automatically — Modify during the request, DINE shortly after the resource is created (about ten minutes later by default). Existing resources, and anything evaluated while the assignment was in DoNotEnforce, need a remediation task, which fixes one Modify or DINE policy at a time, so for an initiative you name the policy's reference ID.

Warning: The classic at-scale remediation failure: a DINE policy assigned at the Landing zones group must send diagnostic logs to log-nusa in the Management subscription. Its identity has roles inside Landing zones, but none on the workspace, so every remediation deployment fails with an authorization error. Grant the identity the roles it needs on every scope it writes to — including scopes outside the assignment.

No baseline fits every case, so you need a documented way to say "not here". A policy exemption marks a scope (from a management group down to a single resource) as exempt from an assignment, or from chosen policies inside an initiative. It shows up in compliance as Exempt, can carry an expiry date and metadata such as a ticket number, and comes in two categories:

| Exemption: Waiver | Exemption: Mitigated | Exclusion (notScopes)
Meaning | The risk is known and accepted for now | The policy's intent is met another way | The scope is simply not evaluated
Nusantara example | The loyalty beta may use West Europe for 30 days while a partner integration is tested | A VM that policy expects in Azure Backup is already protected by the Sulawesi chain's backup product | A lab resource group nobody reports on
Visible in compliance | Yes, as Exempt | Yes, as Exempt | No
Built-in expiry | Optional expiresOn | Optional expiresOn | None

An expired exemption is not deleted; it simply stops applying, and the resource reappears as non-compliant. Creating an exemption needs permission to write exemptions and the exempt action on the assignment (the built-in Resource Policy Contributor role has both), so decide deliberately who may grant exceptions.

Finally, regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud builds on the same machinery. The Microsoft cloud security benchmark is enabled by default, and you can add standards such as ISO/IEC 27001:2022, PCI DSS v4.0.1 or NIST SP 800-53. On Azure these standards are policy initiatives behind the scenes, so the same inheritance rules apply. The dashboard maps technical controls to recommendations; it supports an audit, but it does not certify you. Some standards or features may require a paid Defender plan — check the documentation before promising a report to the auditors.

4. Governance as code — and life after Blueprints

Clicking policies into the portal works for ten assignments, not for two hundred. Policy as code treats definitions, initiatives, assignments and exemptions as files in Git: every change is a pull request, reviewed by a second person, deployed by a pipeline whose identity is the only one allowed to write policy resources. Microsoft's guidance suggests a folder per initiative with files such as policyset.json, policyset.definitions.json and policyset.parameters.json, plus assign.<name>.json files and an exemptions.<name>/ folder. Existing definitions and assignments can be exported with the CLI, PowerShell or Resource Graph, so you can start from what already exists. Larger teams often adopt the open-source Enterprise Policy as Code (EPAC) project, or the policy library that ships with the Azure landing zone accelerators.

The Azure landing zone accelerators package all of this: the hierarchy, the platform subscriptions and a curated policy set, deployed through an infrastructure-as-code accelerator (Bicep or Terraform, built on Azure Verified Modules and wired to GitHub or Azure DevOps) or a portal experience for a first try. Most companies start from an accelerator and adjust, rather than designing from a blank page.

That brings us to Rizky's blueprint. Azure Blueprints (preview) is being retired in phases: no new blueprint definitions from July 31, 2026, no new assignments from October 31, 2026, no changes to existing assignments from December 31, 2026, and full retirement on January 31, 2027. The replacement is a pair of tools you met in Lunch 20: deployment stacks, which deploy and track a set of resources at resource group, subscription or management group scope and can protect them with deny settings; and template specs (or Git) to store and version the templates.

Blueprint concept | Replacement
Blueprint definition and its versions | Bicep or ARM templates in Git, optionally published as template specs with versions
Policy assignment artifact | Policy assignment resources in the template — or your policy-as-code repository
Role assignment artifact | Role assignment resources in the template, assigned to groups
Resource group and template artifacts | Resource groups and modules in the template, deployed at subscription scope
Blueprint assignment | A deployment stack, for example az stack mg create targeting a subscription
Blueprint resource locks | The stack's deny settings (denyDelete or denyWriteAndDelete), with a few excluded principals

Important: On January 31, 2027 the Blueprints service stops. Deployed resources stay, but definitions and assignments you did not export are removed, and blueprint locks stop protecting your resources. Export, convert to Bicep, and redeploy as deployment stacks with deny settings before that date.

5. Seeing everything: Resource Graph at scale and Azure Arc

Governance you cannot see is wishful thinking. Azure Resource Graph answers questions across every subscription you can read in one query, using a subset of KQL (Lunch 30). Besides the resources table, resourcecontainers holds management groups, subscriptions and resource groups, and policyresources holds compliance states, assignments and exemptions — so "which resources are non-compliant, by initiative, across the company?" is a single query instead of a loop over subscriptions. You can scope a query to a management group, and the CLI returns the first 100 rows unless you ask for more.

policyresources
| where type == 'microsoft.policyinsights/policystates'
| where tostring(properties.complianceState) == 'NonCompliant'
| summarize resources = count() by assignment = tostring(properties.policyAssignmentName)

The forty store servers will never move to Azure, but they can still be governed by it. Azure Arc projects machines and clusters that run elsewhere into Azure Resource Manager, so they get a resource ID, live in a resource group, carry tags and inherit RBAC and policy like any other resource.

Azure Arc for | How it connects | Governance you gain | Cost note
Servers (Windows and Linux, on premises or other clouds) | The Connected Machine agent; a heartbeat every five minutes, shown as Disconnected after 15–30 minutes of silence | Inventory, tags, RBAC, Resource Graph; machine configuration audits settings inside the OS; Update Manager, Defender for Servers, Azure Monitor Agent | The inventory and organisation features are free; add-on services are billed (see each pricing page)
Kubernetes clusters (any CNCF-conformant cluster) | Cluster agents deployed with the CLI | Azure Policy for Kubernetes (built on Gatekeeper), GitOps configuration with Flux, Defender for Containers | Inventory and organisation are free; several extensions are billed (check the Azure Arc pricing page)

A machine that stays disconnected for 45 days can become Expired and must be reconnected by an administrator, so monitor agent status as part of operations. Arc is not for Azure VMs — they are already in Azure Resource Manager.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Here is the plan you take to Ibu Sari. Create the intermediate root nusa with Platform, Landing zones (Corp, Online), Sandboxes and Decommissioned. Move the seven subscriptions in, set Sandboxes as the default management group, and require authorization for hierarchy changes. Put the policy definitions and the initiative in a Git repository with a pipeline, and assign them like this:

Scope | Assignment | Effects | Identity
nusa (intermediate root) | Nusantara baseline: allowed locations (indonesiacentral, southeastasia), required costCenter tag, tag inherited from the resource group | Deny, Modify | System-assigned, with the role the definition names (Contributor) at nusa
nusa | Microsoft cloud security benchmark (Defender for Cloud) | Audit, AuditIfNotExists | None needed
Landing zones | Diagnostic settings to log-nusa | DeployIfNotExists | User-assigned: Monitoring Contributor at Landing zones, Log Analytics Contributor on the workspace
Corp | Customer data stays in Jakarta (allowed locations: indonesiacentral only); no public IP addresses on network interfaces | Deny | None needed

Sandboxes inherit only the baseline, plus a small budget on every sandbox subscription. Everything starts in DoNotEnforce mode. After a week of reading compliance in Resource Graph, you remediate the missing tags, then enforce ring by ring. The loyalty beta gets a Waiver with a 30-day expiry and Ibu Sari's name in the metadata. Before January 31, 2027, Rizky's blueprint becomes a Bicep file deployed as a deployment stack with denyDelete. The forty store servers join through Azure Arc into a dedicated subscription under Corp, so the same baseline, tags and Update Manager reach them. The Sulawesi subscriptions wait outside the intermediate root until their West Europe resources have a migration plan — then they move in.

Pause and think: the Sulawesi subscriptions arrive with storage accounts in West Europe. If you moved them under nusa today, with the baseline enforced, what would happen to those existing accounts — and to the next deployment their team tries in West Europe?

Today's lab builds a small version of this design in your own tenant, and the advanced capstone challenge then asks you to put a policy initiative around a complete solution.

Field notes from Stefanus

Ask where the next subscription lands. In every governance review I start with one question: if someone creates a subscription this afternoon, where does it land, and which rules apply to it in its first minute? If the honest answer is "under the tenant root, nothing yet", the hierarchy is only a diagram. Then I look for side doors, because the trap I see most often is not a missing policy but an unguarded exit: who may move subscriptions, who may grant exemptions, and does every exemption have an owner and an end date? Finally, before any Deny goes live at the intermediate root, I write its non-compliance message in plain words: what was blocked, why, and whom to ask. Someone who hits a bare error at six in the evening looks for a workaround, not for the policy owner.

Go further

- Cloud Adoption Framework: Management groups (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/design-area/resource-org-management-groups) — the landing zone hierarchy and the design recommendations behind it
- Design Azure Policy as Code workflows (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/governance/policy/concepts/policy-as-code) — file layout, testing with DoNotEnforce and remediation in a pipeline
- Migrate blueprints to deployment stacks (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/migrate-blueprint) — how each blueprint artifact becomes Bicep under a deployment stack
- What is Azure Arc-enabled servers? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-arc/servers/overview) — the Connected Machine agent and what you can govern outside Azure

quiz.q: Dewi creates a new subscription with her Visual Studio benefit. It appears under the tenant root group and none of the baseline policies apply to it. Which setting would have prevented this?
quiz.a: A default management group in the hierarchy settings (for example Sandboxes). New subscriptions land under the tenant root group unless a default is configured, so without it they start outside every inherited rule.

quiz.q: You saved a custom initiative in the storefront production subscription. Assigning it at the Landing zones management group fails. Why, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: A definition can only be assigned at or below the scope where it is saved. Save the initiative at the intermediate root (or at Landing zones) and assign that copy — the definition's location decides where it can be used.

quiz.q: A DeployIfNotExists assignment at Landing zones should send diagnostic logs to log-nusa in the Management subscription. Its remediation tasks fail with authorization errors. What is missing?
quiz.a: A role for the assignment's managed identity on the workspace (for example Log Analytics Contributor). The identity only has roles inside the assignment scope, but the deployment writes outside it — every target scope needs a grant.

quiz.q: Ibu Sari accepts that the loyalty beta may keep a storage account in West Europe for 30 days while a partner tests an integration. How do you record this so it stays visible and does not become permanent?
quiz.a: Create a policy exemption with category Waiver, scoped to the beta's resource group (or the single resource), with expiresOn set 30 days ahead and metadata naming the approver and ticket. A Waiver means an accepted risk; it remains visible as Exempt, and after expiry the resource shows as non-compliant again.

quiz.q: It is February 2027. Rizky's blueprint was never migrated. What happened to the resources it deployed and to the blueprint locks protecting them?
quiz.a: The resources still exist, but the blueprint assignment and its locks are gone, so nothing prevents someone from deleting them. Redeploy the same templates as a deployment stack with deny settings (and keep the templates in Git or template specs) — the replacement Microsoft recommends.

takeaways: Design the management group hierarchy for inheritance of policy and access: an intermediate root with Platform, Landing zones (Corp, Online, Local), Sandboxes and Decommissioned, three or four levels deep, grouped by workload type.
Subscriptions are the unit of scale; subscription vending places each new one in the right management group with networking, group-based RBAC, budgets and tags before any workload arrives.
Save definitions high, assign initiatives at management-group scope with parameters, start in DoNotEnforce, and give Modify and DeployIfNotExists identities roles on every scope they write to.
Exemptions (Waiver or Mitigated) with expiry dates and metadata keep exceptions visible and auditable; exclusions silently remove scopes from the report.

Governance is code: Git, pipelines, deployment stacks and template specs replace Blueprints before January 31, 2027, while Resource Graph and Azure Arc extend visibility and control to every subscription and to servers outside Azure.

lab.title: Governance for the whole company
lab.text:
What you'll build

Ibu Sari wants the same rules in every subscription Nusantara Retail will ever own. You will build a miniature Azure landing zone hierarchy of management groups, write a custom initiative as code (allowed locations, a required costCenter tag and the same tag inherited from the resource group), assign it the safe way — DoNotEnforce first, with a managed identity — fix existing resources with a remediation task, give Dewi's sandbox experiment a time-boxed Waiver, read compliance across scopes with Azure Resource Graph, and export everything as policy-as-code files. Moving your subscription into the hierarchy is optional (Path B) and fully reversible.

Before you start

- Your own tenant. Management groups are tenant-wide objects. Do this lab only in a Microsoft Entra tenant you control — for example the one created with your free account — in a subscription where you are Owner. Never run it in your employer's tenant, and never move a company subscription. If your organisation gave you a sandbox tenant for learning, check with its administrators first.
- In a new tenant, any user can create management groups. If your tenant's hierarchy settings require authorization, Task 2 fails with AuthorizationFailed — use another tenant.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings plus this lab's names:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/31-governance-at-scale
source ../common/config.sh
source lab-vars.sh        # resource groups, management group names, policy names, Path A/B
echo "Path $LAB31_PATH | corp RG: $CORP_RG | sandbox RG: $SANDBOX_RG | intermediate root: $MG_ROOT"

- Create the starting point — two resource groups with untagged "legacy" resources (about 2–3 minutes). The script shows your tenant and subscription and asks you to confirm that they are yours:

bash setup.sh

Important: The lab costs almost nothing (an empty storage account and two network security groups), but it creates objects outside resource groups: management groups, an initiative, a policy assignment, an exemption and a role assignment. Always finish with the Clean up section — cleanup.sh removes all of them, in the right order, and moves your subscription back if you moved it.

Tip: Cloud Shell forgets your variables when it times out. Go back to the lab folder and run source ../common/config.sh && source lab-vars.sh again. Do the same after Task 3: the variables then switch to Path B.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–9 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Both modes work on one of two paths. Choose before Task 3:

| Path A (default) | Path B (optional)
Your subscription | stays where it is | moves into mg-nusa-corp-<suffix> in Task 3
Initiative saved at | your subscription | the intermediate root mg-nusa-<suffix>
Initiative assigned at | your subscription | mg-nusa-landingzones-<suffix> — your subscription inherits it
What you learn | everything except real inheritance through management groups | the full landing-zone pattern: save high, assign at landing zones, inherit downwards
You need | Owner on the subscription | Owner on the subscription, in a tenant you own
Undo | nothing to undo | cleanup.sh moves the subscription back to its original parent

Why the difference? A definition can only be assigned at or below the scope where it is saved. While your subscription sits outside mg-nusa-<suffix>, an initiative saved in that management group cannot reach it, so Path A saves the initiative in the subscription itself.

Task 1 · Look at the starting point and find the built-ins

Start by seeing what you are about to govern, and find the three built-in definitions the initiative will reuse.

for rg in "$CORP_RG" "$SANDBOX_RG"; do
  echo "== $rg  (resource group costCenter: $(az group show --name "$rg" --query tags.costCenter --output tsv))"
  az resource list --resource-group "$rg" \
    --query "[].{name:name, type:type, location:location, costCenter:tags.costCenter}" --output table
done

lookup_builtin_ids     # from lab-vars.sh: looks the definitions up by display name, never by GUID
printf '%s\n' "$ALLOWED_LOCATIONS_ID" "$REQUIRE_TAG_ID" "$INHERIT_TAG_ID"

The corp group carries costCenter=CC-2001, but its storage account and network security group do not. The sandbox group has no tag at all, and its network security group sits in $SECONDARY_LOCATION — outside the region the baseline will allow.

Checkpoint: three legacy resources with an empty costCenter column, and three IDs that start with /providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions/. If an ID is empty, run lookup_builtin_ids again.

Task 2 · Build the management group hierarchy

You will create the smallest piece of the Azure landing zone hierarchy that still shows the pattern: an intermediate root under the tenant root group, a Platform group, a Landing zones group and Corp below it.

az account management-group create --name "$MG_ROOT" --display-name "Nusantara Retail (lab $SUFFIX)"
az account management-group create --name "$MG_PLATFORM" --display-name "Platform" --parent "$MG_ROOT"
az account management-group create --name "$MG_LZ" --display-name "Landing zones" --parent "$MG_ROOT"
az account management-group create --name "$MG_CORP" --display-name "Corp" --parent "$MG_LZ"

A few things worth knowing while the commands run:

- The --name is the management group's ID. It can never change; the display name can. That is why the lab adds your suffix to every ID.
- The very first management group in a tenant can take up to 15 minutes to appear. If a child fails with "not found", wait a minute and run that line again.
- You become Owner of every management group you create, which is what lets you save and assign policies there.
- A real landing zone has more groups (Security, Management, Connectivity and Identity under Platform; Online and Local next to Corp; Sandboxes; Decommissioned). Lunch 31 explains each one.

for mg in "$MG_ROOT" "$MG_PLATFORM" "$MG_LZ" "$MG_CORP"; do
  echo "$mg  ->  parent: $(mg_parent "$mg")"
done

Tip: Prefer the portal? Portal path: Home › Management groups › + Create. Then select Tenant root group and expand the tree to see your four groups — the portal shows the hierarchy better than any command.

Checkpoint: the intermediate root's parent is your tenant ID (the tenant root group); platform and landing zones point to mg-nusa-<suffix>; corp points to mg-nusa-landingzones-<suffix>.

Task 3 · (Optional, Path B) Move your lab subscription into Corp

Skip this task for Path A. For Path B, read this first.

Warning: Moving a subscription changes which policies and role assignments apply to everything in it, and Azure can take up to 30 minutes to reflect the new hierarchy everywhere. Do it only with your own lab subscription in your own tenant. In a personal tenant the subscription normally sits directly under the tenant root group, so moving it out and back needs no extra permissions.

# 1. Where does the subscription live now? (The tenant root group's ID is your tenant ID.)
ORIGINAL_PARENT=$(az graph query --graph-query "resourcecontainers
  | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' and subscriptionId == '$SUB_ID'
  | project parent = tostring(properties.managementGroupAncestorsChain[0].name)" \
  --query "data[0].parent" --output tsv)
echo "Current parent: ${ORIGINAL_PARENT:-$TENANT_ID}"

# 2. Move it into Corp
az account management-group subscription add --name "$MG_CORP" --subscription "$SUB_ID"

# 3. Remember the original parent for cleanup.sh, then reload the lab variables (they switch to Path B)
echo "${ORIGINAL_PARENT:-$TENANT_ID}" > "$LAB31_STATE_FILE"
source lab-vars.sh && echo "Path $LAB31_PATH: assign at $ASSIGN_SCOPE"

If az graph asks to install the resource-graph extension, answer yes (setup.sh normally installed it already).

Checkpoint: az account management-group subscription show --name "$MG_CORP" --subscription "$SUB_ID" --query displayName --output tsv prints your subscription's name, and echo $LAB31_PATH prints B.

Task 4 · Create the initiative from policy-as-code files

Open the two files in policy/nusa-baseline/. They follow the layout from Microsoft's policy-as-code guidance:

cat policy/nusa-baseline/policyset.definitions.json   # the three member policies
cat policy/nusa-baseline/policyset.parameters.json    # the initiative's own parameters

Each member has a short reference ID (allowedLocations, requireCostCenterTag, inheritCostCenterTag) and passes an initiative parameter through to the policy — [parameters('allowedLocations')] becomes the built-in's listOfAllowedLocations. The definition IDs are placeholders, because the course never hard-codes GUIDs: render them with the IDs you looked up in Task 1, then create the initiative.

mkdir -p generated
sed -e "s#__ALLOWED_LOCATIONS_ID__#${ALLOWED_LOCATIONS_ID}#" \
    -e "s#__REQUIRE_TAG_ID__#${REQUIRE_TAG_ID}#" \
    -e "s#__INHERIT_TAG_ID__#${INHERIT_TAG_ID}#" \
    policy/nusa-baseline/policyset.definitions.json > generated/policyset.definitions.json

az policy set-definition create --name "$INITIATIVE" $INITIATIVE_SCOPE_FLAG \
  --display-name "Nusantara baseline" \
  --description "Allowed locations, a required costCenter tag, and the costCenter tag inherited from the resource group." \
  --definitions ./generated/policyset.definitions.json \
  --params ./policy/nusa-baseline/policyset.parameters.json

$INITIATIVE_SCOPE_FLAG is empty on Path A (the initiative is saved in your subscription) and --management-group mg-nusa-<suffix> on Path B (saved at the intermediate root, so every group below can use it).

Checkpoint: az policy set-definition show --name "$INITIATIVE" $INITIATIVE_SCOPE_FLAG --query "policyDefinitions[].policyDefinitionReferenceId" lists the three reference IDs. If the command says it cannot find the initiative, run source lab-vars.sh — the path variables may be out of date.

Task 5 · Assign the initiative — safely

Assign the initiative once, at the top of what you govern: your subscription (Path A) or the landing zones group (Path B). Two choices make this assignment safe and useful.

az policy assignment create --name "$ASSIGNMENT" --display-name "Nusantara baseline (Lab 31)" \
  --scope "$ASSIGN_SCOPE" --policy-set-definition "$INITIATIVE_ID" \
  --params "{ 'allowedLocations': { 'value': [ '$LOCATION' ] }, 'tagName': { 'value': 'costCenter' } }" \
  --enforcement-mode DoNotEnforce \
  --mi-system-assigned --location "$LOCATION" \
  --identity-scope "$CORP_RG_ID" --role Contributor

- --enforcement-mode DoNotEnforce — Azure evaluates and reports compliance, but denies and modifies nothing while resources are created or updated. Remediation tasks still work. This is the first ring of a safe rollout.
- --mi-system-assigned --location — the Modify policy inside the initiative needs a managed identity to change resources. --identity-scope and --role grant it Contributor (the role the built-in definition asks for) on the corp group only. In production you would grant it everywhere remediation must write, usually the assignment scope.

Warning: On Path A this assignment covers your whole subscription. In DoNotEnforce mode it only reports, which is why you may see resources from other labs listed as non-compliant. Do not switch it to Default enforcement: the required-tag policy would then refuse every untagged resource in the subscription, including other labs. The stretch goals show a safe way to try enforcement.

Checkpoint: the assignment reports DoNotEnforce and a system-assigned identity, and the identity holds a role on the corp group:

az policy assignment show --name "$ASSIGNMENT" --scope "$ASSIGN_SCOPE" \
  --query "{mode:enforcementMode, identity:identity.type, locations:parameters.allowedLocations.value}"
PID=$(az policy assignment show --name "$ASSIGNMENT" --scope "$ASSIGN_SCOPE" --query identity.principalId --output tsv)
az role assignment list --scope "$CORP_RG_ID" --query "[?principalId=='$PID'].roleDefinitionName" --output tsv

If the last command prints nothing, wait a minute (new identities take a moment to replicate) and grant it yourself: az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role Contributor --scope "$CORP_RG_ID".

Task 6 · Remediate the corp resource group

The assignment does not touch existing resources by itself. A remediation task does — for one Modify or DeployIfNotExists policy at a time, so for an initiative you name the member's reference ID. ReEvaluateCompliance makes the task check the resources now instead of waiting for the next compliance scan.

az policy remediation create --name "$REMEDIATION" --resource-group "$CORP_RG" \
  --policy-assignment "$ASSIGNMENT_ID" --definition-reference-id inheritCostCenterTag \
  --resource-discovery-mode ReEvaluateCompliance

# Run this every minute or so until the state is Succeeded (usually 5–15 minutes)
az policy remediation show --name "$REMEDIATION" --resource-group "$CORP_RG" \
  --query "{state:provisioningState, deployments:deploymentStatus}"

az resource list --resource-group "$CORP_RG" --query "[].{name:name, costCenter:tags.costCenter}" --output table

While you wait, think about the sandbox: why will this task never touch it? (Its resource group has no costCenter tag to inherit, and the identity has no role there.)

Checkpoint: the remediation state is Succeeded, and both stcorp<suffix> and nsg-corp-legacy now show CC-2001. If the state is Succeeded but the tags are missing, the resources were not yet evaluated — create a second task with another --name, for example "${REMEDIATION}-2".

Task 7 · Grant the sandbox a time-boxed Waiver

Dewi's experiment breaks two rules: it sits in $SECONDARY_LOCATION and has no costCenter tag. Ibu Sari accepts that risk for 30 days while a partner integration is tested. That is a Waiver: an accepted risk, visible in compliance as Exempt, with an end date and a paper trail.

EXPIRES=$(date -u -d '+30 days' '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
az policy exemption create --name "$EXEMPTION" --resource-group "$SANDBOX_RG" \
  --policy-assignment "$ASSIGNMENT_ID" --exemption-category Waiver --expires-on "$EXPIRES" \
  --display-name "Sandbox experiment in $SECONDARY_LOCATION (NUSA-1042)" \
  --description "Dewi tests a partner integration for 30 days. Risk accepted by Ibu Sari." \
  --metadata "{requestedBy:Dewi,approvedBy:'Ibu Sari',ticketRef:NUSA-1042}"

Tip: Use Mitigated instead of Waiver when the policy's intent is met another way. To exempt a scope from only some members of an initiative, add --policy-definition-reference-ids with their reference IDs. And when an exemption expires, Azure does not delete it — the resources simply show as non-compliant again.

Checkpoint: az policy exemption list --resource-group "$SANDBOX_RG" --query "[].{name:name, category:exemptionCategory, expires:expiresOn}" --output table shows one Waiver that expires in 30 days.

Task 8 · Read compliance at scale with Resource Graph

Ask Azure to evaluate both lab groups now, instead of waiting for the next scheduled cycle:

az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "$CORP_RG" --no-wait
az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "$SANDBOX_RG" --no-wait

# Repeat until both numbers are above zero (often 5–10 minutes)
for rg in "$CORP_RG" "$SANDBOX_RG"; do
  echo "$rg: $(az policy state list --resource-group "$rg" --filter "policyAssignmentName eq '$ASSIGNMENT'" --query "length(@)" --output tsv) records"
done

Now query compliance the way a platform team does — across every subscription you can read, in one request. Resource Graph can lag a few minutes behind the commands above.

# 1. The initiative's results by member policy and state
az graph query --graph-query "policyresources
  | where type == 'microsoft.policyinsights/policystates'
  | where tostring(properties.policyAssignmentName) == '$ASSIGNMENT'
  | summarize resources = count() by policy = tostring(properties.policyDefinitionReferenceId), state = tostring(properties.complianceState)
  | order by policy asc" --query data --output table

# 2. Which lab resources are still non-compliant, and why?
az graph query --graph-query "policyresources
  | where type == 'microsoft.policyinsights/policystates'
  | where tostring(properties.policyAssignmentName) == '$ASSIGNMENT'
  | where tostring(properties.complianceState) == 'NonCompliant'
  | where tolower(tostring(properties.resourceId)) contains '/resourcegroups/rg-lunch31-'
  | project resource = extract('[^/]+$', 0, tostring(properties.resourceId)), policy = tostring(properties.policyDefinitionReferenceId)" \
  --query data --output table

# 3. Every exemption you can see, with its category and end date
az graph query --graph-query "policyresources
  | where type == 'microsoft.authorization/policyexemptions'
  | project name, resourceGroup, category = tostring(properties.exemptionCategory), expiresOn = tostring(properties.expiresOn)" \
  --query data --output table

# 4. Where each of your subscriptions sits in the hierarchy
az graph query --graph-query "resourcecontainers
  | where type == 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions'
  | project subscription = name, parent = tostring(properties.managementGroupAncestorsChain[0].displayName)" \
  --query data --output table

On Path B, add --management-groups "$MG_ROOT" to any query to limit it to the lab hierarchy, and try az policy state summarize --management-group "$MG_LZ" for a roll-up at management-group scope.

Checkpoint: the corp resources are Compliant for all three members, query 2 lists nothing from the corp group, query 3 shows sandbox-waiver as a Waiver, and query 4 shows your subscription under Corp (Path B) or the tenant root group (Path A). Sandbox resources show as Exempt once they have been evaluated again.

Task 9 · Export the governance as code

Everything you clicked or typed should live in Git, reviewed and deployed by a pipeline. Export the desired state — only the properties you would maintain by hand, not the read-only ones Azure adds — in the policy-as-code layout:

OUT="exported/$INITIATIVE"
mkdir -p "$OUT/exemptions.$ASSIGNMENT"
az policy set-definition show --name "$INITIATIVE" $INITIATIVE_SCOPE_FLAG \
  --query "{name:name, displayName:displayName, description:description, parameters:parameters, policyDefinitions:policyDefinitions}" \
  --output json > "$OUT/policyset.json"
az policy assignment show --name "$ASSIGNMENT" --scope "$ASSIGN_SCOPE" \
  --query "{name:name, displayName:displayName, scope:scope, policyDefinitionId:policyDefinitionId, enforcementMode:enforcementMode, parameters:parameters, nonComplianceMessages:nonComplianceMessages, identityType:identity.type, location:location}" \
  --output json > "$OUT/assign.$ASSIGNMENT.json"
az policy exemption show --name "$EXEMPTION" --resource-group "$SANDBOX_RG" \
  --query "{name:name, displayName:displayName, exemptionCategory:exemptionCategory, expiresOn:expiresOn, policyAssignmentId:policyAssignmentId, metadata:metadata}" \
  --output json > "$OUT/exemptions.$ASSIGNMENT/$EXEMPTION.json"
find exported -type f | sort

In a real team these files go into a repository next to policy/nusa-baseline/, and a pipeline with its own identity deploys them. Here generated/ and exported/ are listed in the lab's .gitignore on purpose: they contain your subscription ID, which does not belong in a public repository.

Checkpoint: three files — policyset.json, assign.nusa-baseline.json and exemptions.nusa-baseline/sandbox-waiver.json — and the assignment file shows "enforcementMode": "DoNotEnforce".

Break it and fix it

Rizky saves a new audit policy in the Corp management group and wants to assign it to the whole Landing zones group. Try it:

az policy definition create --name "$SCOPE_TEST" --management-group "$MG_CORP" \
  --display-name "Lab 31 scope test: audit storage without costCenter" \
  --mode Indexed --rules ./policy/scope-test/policy.rules.json

az policy assignment create --name "$SCOPE_TEST" --scope "$MG_PREFIX/$MG_LZ" \
  --policy "$MG_PREFIX/$MG_CORP/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions/$SCOPE_TEST"

The definition is created, but the assignment fails with an error saying the policy definition is out of scope (definitions can only be used at or below the scope where they are saved). The exact wording can vary between versions.

Hint and fix

The definition lives below the scope you are assigning to. Save it at the Landing zones group (or higher), assign that copy, and delete the copy that was saved too low. The policy only audits, so it changes nothing.

az policy definition create --name "$SCOPE_TEST" --management-group "$MG_LZ" \
  --display-name "Lab 31 scope test: audit storage without costCenter" \
  --mode Indexed --rules ./policy/scope-test/policy.rules.json
az policy assignment create --name "$SCOPE_TEST" --scope "$MG_PREFIX/$MG_LZ" \
  --policy "$MG_PREFIX/$MG_LZ/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions/$SCOPE_TEST"
az policy definition delete --name "$SCOPE_TEST" --management-group "$MG_CORP"

This is the same rule that decides Path A vs Path B, and why landing zone designs save shared definitions at the intermediate root. cleanup.sh removes the assignment and the definition.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. verify.sh works for both paths and changes nothing.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

The order matters, and the script follows it: exemptions, then the identity's role assignment and the policy assignments, then the initiative and definitions, then your subscription moves back to its original parent (Path B), then the management groups — children first — and finally the resource groups rg-lunch31-corp-<suffix> and rg-lunch31-sandbox-<suffix> and the generated/ and exported/ folders. If Azure still sees a child under a management group (its view of the hierarchy can lag after a move), the script retries; if it gives up, wait a few minutes and run it again.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
AuthorizationFailed … Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write in Task 2 | your tenant requires authorization to create management groups, or it is a work tenant | use a tenant you own; do not ask for rights in a company tenant just for this lab
A child management group fails with "not found" right after its parent was created | the first management group in a tenant can take up to 15 minutes; the hierarchy is eventually consistent | wait a minute and run the same command again
AuthorizationFailed when moving the subscription in Task 3 | you need Owner on the subscription and write access on both the current and the new parent (the tenant root group is the exception) | stay on Path A, or use your own tenant
InvalidCreatePolicyAssignmentRequest … out of scope | the definition is saved below the assignment scope (the Break it and fix it task, or a Path A initiative assigned to a management group) | save the definition at or above the scope you assign to
PolicyDefinitionNotFound while creating the initiative | the placeholders were not replaced (Task 1 variables were empty when you ran sed) | run lookup_builtin_ids, re-run the sed command, create the initiative again
The CLI cannot parse --definitions or --params | file-path handling differs between CLI versions | pass the contents instead: --definitions "$(cat generated/policyset.definitions.json)"
PrincipalNotFound when the role is granted in Task 5 | the brand-new managed identity has not replicated in Microsoft Entra ID yet | wait a minute, then run the az role assignment create command from the Task 5 checkpoint
Remediation Failed, or Succeeded with zero deployments | the identity has no role on the corp group, or the resources were not evaluated yet (on Path B, the new hierarchy can take a while to apply) | fix the role, wait a few minutes, create a new remediation task with another --name
az policy exemption create refuses the scope right after a Path B move | Azure's cached view of the hierarchy still places the resource group outside the assignment | wait a few minutes; or add --assignment-scope-validation DoNotValidate
az graph query returns no policy states | Resource Graph lags behind, or no evaluation has finished | run the Task 8 scans, wait a few minutes, query again
'graph' is misspelled or not recognized | the Resource Graph extension is missing | az extension add --name resource-graph
cleanup.sh cannot delete a management group | a child or the subscription is still attached in Azure's cached view | wait a few minutes, then run bash cleanup.sh again

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), after running bash setup.sh:

1. Management groups mg-nusa-<suffix> (under the tenant root group), mg-nusa-platform-<suffix> and mg-nusa-landingzones-<suffix> (both under mg-nusa-<suffix>), and mg-nusa-corp-<suffix> (under landing zones).
2. A custom initiative containing the built-ins Allowed locations, Require a tag on resources and Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing, with initiative parameters for the allowed locations and the tag name — saved in your subscription (Path A) or in mg-nusa-<suffix> (Path B, with your subscription moved into corp).
3. An assignment of that initiative to your subscription (Path A) or to mg-nusa-landingzones-<suffix> (Path B): allowed locations = only $LOCATION, tag name costCenter, enforcement mode DoNotEnforce, and a managed identity that holds Contributor on rg-lunch31-corp-<suffix>.
4. A successful remediation task in rg-lunch31-corp-<suffix>, after which both legacy resources carry costCenter=CC-2001.
5. A Waiver exemption on rg-lunch31-sandbox-<suffix> for that assignment, expiring within 30 days.
6. Compliance records for the assignment in the corp group.
7. The assignment exported as exported/<initiative>/assign.<assignment>.json in the lab folder.
